Here's a basic rundown of the selloff:

  • The market is beholden to central banks due to years of quantitative easing.

  • The correlation between the returns of stocks and bonds is important to observe.

  • Diversification between stocks and bonds only works when this correlation is negative.

  • When bonds sell off too quickly, the return correlation can flip positive.

  • When this happens, equities selloff alongside bonds.

  • Friday's job reports showed higher than expected signs of inflation.

  • If inflation spikes, the Fed will tighten monetary policy faster than previously expected.

  • Anticipating the Fed's action, the market fell.

The whole "Goldilocks" environment in which the current economic climate hinges upon central banks normalizing policy slowly and carefully. A rising tide lifts all boats, and that tide is ~$20,000,000,000,000 in USD injected into the global markets. We're treading into unknown waters as global quantitative easing shifts into quantitative tightening, as nothing on this scale has ever occurred before. QE suppressed the risk premium in fixed income instruments, forcing investors into riskier assets.

An exerpt from a BofAML note:

In 2017, multi-asset portfolios continued to benefit from equity/bond diversification. Low equity/bond correlation alongside record low cross-asset volatility is driving the volume of equity/bond risk parity portfolios to its lowest levels since the 1960s. Other multi-asset portfolios holding a mixture of equities and bonds have likely also seen extremely low volatility recently. However, a disorderly rise in yields that accompanies an equity market pullback (i.e., 2013 Taper Tantrum) could be a surprise for many investors who have become conditioned to the recent environment in which bonds and equities diversify one another.

The correlation of rate-sensitive assets to US rates is at record highs as investors fail to care about outside risks, leaving markets increasingly dependent on US policy. Coupled with rates volume near lifetime-lows - on few expectation for policy disruption - this has helped suppress global cross-asset volume. However, with the Fed appearing to soldier-on towards policy normalization, persistently ow rates volume may be at risk. This in turn creates risks for a market slaved to rates.

Two years ago, the Fed began tightening very slowly. As long as inflation remains subdued then they can't yank away the punch bowl too quickly. However, on Friday the jobs report showed a very positive average hourly earnings gains leading to concerns about a marked uptick in wage pressures. Wage pressures are one of the key areas which we haven't seen inflation in years. If inflation spikes unexpectedly and the Fed is slow behind the curve, they will tighten monetary policy at a faster pace. This is negative for risk assets.

The other factor is the correlation between stocks and bonds. Typically, both move inversely to one another as the former is riskier than the latter. When investors are bullish on the future and "risk-on" is alive, you would expect to see flows out of bonds and into stocks (Trump being elected).

When the return correlation between stocks and bonds flips positive, the two asset classes may sell off together and such a diversified portfolio may not staunch the bleeding. Most people will reference the US 10-yr Treasury bond yields as a benchmark or a thermometer of sorts since bond prices and yields move inversely. Rising bond yields can be a good thing, as it means investors are selling bonds and (hopefully) moving into equities or riskier instruments. There is, however, a point at which a bond market selloff moves too quickly, yields spike faster than expected, and investors interpret that as a panic signal.

The T-note selloff which caused yields to rise above comfort levels of many investors combined with perceived wage pressure in the jobs report spooked the market.
